Cross: the Lamb takes the scroll
Christ's victory qualifies him to open the sealed scroll of history (Revelation 5); Daniel's seventy weeks are usually fulfilled in his ministry.
The apostolic church begins the history Revelation will chart.
Most historicists read much of the Olivet Discourse as fulfilled in AD 70, but date Revelation c. AD 95 (a disputed date), so its visions begin after Jerusalem's fall.
Seals and trumpets: pagan Rome to the Turks

In Elliott's widely followed scheme the seals trace pagan Rome from prosperity to Constantine (c. 312); the first four trumpets are the barbarian invasions that toppled the western empire (c. 400–476); the fifth and sixth are the Saracen and Ottoman Turkish woes, ending with the fall of Constantinople (1453).
1,260 years: the papal Antichrist

Using the day-year principle, the 1,260 days, 42 months and 'time, times and half a time' are read as 1,260 years of papal dominance. A common reckoning ran from Justinian's decree (533/538) to the French capture of Pope Pius VI (1798); others proposed 606–1866. The Westminster Confession (1646) named the pope as the man of sin. The papal power's persecution of faithful believers is this view's Great Tribulation.
Reformation: the little open book and the two witnesses
The angel with the open book (Revelation 10) is read as the recovery of the Bible in the Reformation (1517), and the witnesses' resurrection (Revelation 11) as the revival of Protestant testimony.
Bowls (vials): judgments on the papal and Ottoman powers

Many nineteenth-century historicists saw the bowls poured out from the French Revolution onward, with the drying of the Euphrates as the Ottoman empire's decline. Historicists today usually place the present near the end of the sequence.
Conversion of the Jews
Puritan historicists widely expected a future national conversion of the Jews, which would spark worldwide revival, a hope that drove early Protestant missions (Iain Murray's 'Puritan Hope').
Millennium: the latter-day glory

Postmillennial historicists (Edwards, many Puritans) expected a future era of gospel triumph after Antichrist's fall, before Christ returns. Premillennial historicists (Elliott, Guinness, Spurgeon) instead placed the Second Coming at its start. Some earlier historicists (and Augustine-influenced Reformers) read the millennium as already past or present.
One personal return of Christ, after a brief final apostasy (postmillennial historicism), with the general resurrection.
Resurrection and final judgment
General resurrection and the great white throne.
New Jerusalem
The eternal state and the bride of the Lamb.

Futurism reads most of Revelation (chapters 4–22) and the final week of Daniel's seventy weeks as describing events still to come at the end of the age. It is associated with dispensationalism (Walvoord, Pentecost, Ryrie) but is not restricted to it: historic premillennialists such as Ladd are futurists, as are prewrath advocates (Rosenthal, Kurschner). Early Church Fathers (Irenaeus, Hippolytus) and the Jesuit Francisco Ribera (16th century) also read Revelation's climax as future. This chart shows the most common (pre-tribulational) futurist sequence.
Cross
Christ's first coming fulfils the first sixty-nine weeks of Daniel 9 and secures redemption.
The church age begins.
Church age (Revelation 1–3)

Revelation 1:19 is read as a three-part outline: what John saw, 'the things that are' (the seven churches, chapters 2–3), and 'what will take place after this' (chapters 4–22). Some futurists also see the seven letters as a preview of church-age eras.
Fall of Jerusalem: a partial, near fulfilment

Futurists generally grant that Luke 21:20-24 describes AD 70, but argue that the cosmic signs, the worldwide scope and the visible return in Matthew 24 were not fulfilled then. Some see AD 70 as a preview of the end.
Rapture (timing debated)

Most popular futurists hold a pre-tribulation rapture, sometimes linked with John being called up in Revelation 4:1; mid-tribulation, prewrath (before the Day of the Lord, within the week) and post-tribulation futurists place it later.
Future tribulation (Revelation 6–19)
The seals, trumpets and bowls describe literal, global judgments during a final seven-year period (Daniel's seventieth week), with the Great Tribulation proper in its second half.
Future Antichrist and rebuilt temple
A future world ruler (the beast) breaks a covenant with Israel at the midpoint, sets up the abomination of desolation and demands worship for 42 months.
Visible return (Revelation 19)
Christ returns to earth, destroys the beast and false prophet, and begins his reign.
Israel's national repentance
A future mass turning of Israel to Christ at his appearing, held by most futurists, dispensational or not.
Millennium follows the return
Reading Revelation 19–20 in sequence, futurists place the binding of Satan and the thousand-year reign after the Second Coming.
Great white throne
After Satan's last rebellion, the dead are judged.
Revelation 21–22 describes the eternal state.

Idealism (also called the spiritual or symbolic approach) reads Revelation not as a code for particular dated events but as a symbolic portrayal of the timeless conflict between Christ and Satan, the church and the world, which recurs throughout the whole age. The visions repeat this conflict in parallel cycles (Hendriksen's 'progressive parallelism'), each ending with judgment and victory. Most idealists still affirm a real future consummation; this chart therefore shows mostly spans covering the whole church age, followed by the end. Pure idealism (e.g. William Milligan) gives less weight to any single final period than modified forms do.
The Lamb's victory
The slain and standing Lamb (Revelation 5) is the key to the book: the decisive battle is already won, and every later vision is read in its light.
Dragon cast down and bound
Revelation 12 (the dragon thrown down) and Revelation 20 (the dragon bound) are parallel portrayals of Satan's defeat at Christ's first coming.
Millennium: the reign of the saints
The thousand years symbolize the completeness of Christ's reign and of the martyrs' vindication during the whole age; idealists are usually amillennial.
The church, symbolized by the lampstands and the woman of Revelation 12, begins its witness in the wilderness.
Tribulation in every generation
The seals, trumpets and bowls are not consecutive stages but recurring patterns of war, famine, persecution and judgment that run through every era, each cycle ending at the final judgment.
The beast: persecuting power in every age

The sea-beast stands for any state or political power that claims divine authority and persecutes the faithful; the land-beast (false prophet) is false religion and ideology serving it. Rome was the first readers' example, but not the only one.
Babylon the harlot: the seductive world-system
Babylon represents the world's economic and cultural seduction in every age, and the call to 'come out of her' applies in every generation.
AD 70 as one instance
Idealists do not tie Revelation to Jerusalem's fall; most date it c. AD 95 (a disputed date). Judgments such as AD 70 are treated as historical examples of the pattern the book reveals.
Final intensification
Many idealists, Hendriksen among them, see the cycles growing more intense toward the end, with Satan's 'little season' and a final assault on the church.
Christ's return and consummation
The rider on the white horse ends the conflict once for all. Each parallel cycle of visions closes here.
The general resurrection and the great white throne.
The goal toward which every cycle points: God dwelling with his people.

The eclectic (or 'redemptive-historical idealist') approach, defended by G. K. Beale and Dennis Johnson and used in varying ways by Craig Keener and Grant Osborne, combines the strengths of the other approaches. Revelation spoke to first-century churches about Rome (preterist), portrays transhistorical patterns of the whole age in parallel cycles (idealist), and climaxes in a real future consummation (futurist). Beale is amillennial; Osborne, a more futurist-leaning eclectic, is premillennial. This chart follows Beale's amillennial version.
Cross: the Lamb's victory inaugurates the end
Beale stresses inaugurated eschatology: the 'latter days' of Daniel began with Christ's death and resurrection (Revelation 1:1 echoes Daniel 2:28-29).
Satan is restrained from deceiving the nations so that the gospel can spread, in parallel with his casting down in Revelation 12.
Millennium: the inter-advent age
Revelation 20 recapitulates the church age; the saints reign with Christ from heaven while the church suffers on earth.
The church, the true Israel and a kingdom of priests, begins its prophetic witness (the two witnesses as the church).
Parallel cycles of visions
Seals, trumpets and bowls recapitulate the same period from different angles, each with a first-century reference point and an end-time climax.
Tribulation already and not yet
The church is already in the tribulation (Revelation 1:9), which climaxes in a final, more intense persecution before Christ returns.
First-century setting

The first readers would have recognized Rome and the imperial cult in the beast and Babylon. Beale dates Revelation c. AD 95 (the date is disputed) and does not make AD 70 the book's main subject, though the Olivet Discourse's near fulfilment is widely acknowledged.
Final Antichrist embodiment
The beast was embodied in Rome and recurs in later persecuting powers, culminating in a final antichristian manifestation at the end of history.
The one return of Christ, the final battle of Revelation 16, 19 and 20 seen from three angles.
One bodily resurrection of all at the end.
The great white throne judgment.
New creation as cosmic temple
Beale reads the New Jerusalem as the end-time temple filling the whole renewed creation, completing the Eden mandate.

The Spiritual Understanding places the decisive event at the start of the chart: the cross, where 'It is finished' sealed the victory the rest of Revelation unfolds. The Spirit, new birth and new creation begin at Pentecost; the old covenant order is shaken and removed by AD 70; and the whole church age is the thousand-year reign of Christ, in which minds are renewed and Babylon falls wherever the New Jerusalem comes down. Most proponents expect a final appearing that consummates, rather than begins, Christ's victory.
'It is finished': the Lamb as though slain
The cross is the centre of history and the key to the book. The Lion conquers as the slain Lamb, and every later vision unfolds this finished victory.
The accuser cast down
Revelation 12 and Revelation 20 picture the same victory: the accuser of the brothers is thrown down and bound by the blood of the Lamb.
Spirit poured out: new creation begun
The Spirit seals believers with the Father's name; the first resurrection (the new birth) begins, and anyone in Christ is a new creation.
The thousand years: Christ's reign now
The whole age is the fullness of Christ's reign, shared by those raised and seated with him.
Tribulation on the old order
The judgments of the Olivet Discourse fall on the old covenant system and its temple during the Jewish War.
AD 70: end of the old covenant age
What was 'becoming obsolete' passes away; the system of law, temple and mixture gives way to the kingdom that cannot be shaken. Preterist-leaning proponents also see the fall of 'Babylon' here.
Two cities, two minds: ongoing renewal

Throughout the age Babylon (a religion of self-effort and mixture) and the New Jerusalem (the Bride, grace coming down from above) stand side by side. The mark of the beast and the seal of God are two ways of thinking, and minds are renewed as Christ is unveiled.
The Rider conquers by his word
The Rider on the white horse wins the nations with the sword of his mouth, and the harvest of the earth is the fruit of the gospel.
Christ's appearing
Most proponents expect Christ to appear and consummate the victory already won, revealing his people with him in glory.
Death and Hades thrown down
Final judgment completes the cross: the books are opened and death itself is ended (the scope of the lake of fire is interpreted differently within the view).
'It is done': all things new
The New Jerusalem, the Bride, is unveiled in fullness: no more sea, no more curse, and the tree of life (Christ himself) at the centre.
Were all biblical prophecies, including the Second Coming and the bodily resurrection, fulfilled by AD 70?

Full preterists answer yes because of the New Testament's time texts: Jesus promised some standing there would see him coming in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28), said 'this generation' would not pass until all was fulfilled (Matthew 24:34), and Revelation says its events are 'near'. They argue that splitting one coming into two is arbitrary. Everyone else, including partial preterists, answers no. They point to the visible, bodily return promised in Acts 1:11 and the physical resurrection described in 1 Corinthians 15, a hope confessed by every historic creed, and argue that these texts describe events with no first-century counterpart. Note that saying yes places a view outside historic creedal orthodoxy, which proponents accept on the grounds that Scripture outranks the creeds.
Yes: everything was fulfilled in the first century
No: at least Christ's bodily return and the resurrection are still future
Is the thousand years of Revelation 20 a future reign of Christ on earth, beginning after he returns?

Premillennialists read Revelation 19 and 20 in sequence: Christ returns (Revelation 19:11-21), then Satan is bound and the saints 'came to life' and reign (20:1-6). They note that the same verb describes both resurrections in 20:4-5, so if the second is bodily the first should be too, and that the earliest Fathers (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus) were chiliasts. Amillennialists and postmillennialists answer no. They read Revelation as cycles that recapitulate the age, so chapter 20 returns to the first advent; they note that Satan's binding echoes Matthew 12:29, and that elsewhere the New Testament presents one resurrection and judgment 'at the last day' (John 5:28-29), leaving no room for a thousand-year gap.
Yes: Christ returns first, then reigns on earth
No: the millennium is the present age (or a stage within it) before Christ returns
Is Christ's return one event, or two stages (a rapture of the church, then a later return to earth)?

Pre-tribulationists see two stages: in 1 Thessalonians 4 the Lord comes for his saints and takes them to the Father's house (John 14:3), while in Revelation 19 he comes with them to earth. The church is promised exemption from wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9; Revelation 3:10), and the church is not mentioned on earth in Revelation 4–18. Prewrath and midtribulation advocates also see a rapture before the end, but place it within the final seven years, before God's wrath proper begins. Post-tribulationists see one event: Matthew 24:29-31 places the gathering of the elect 'after the tribulation', and the word for 'meeting' (apantēsis) suggests going out to welcome a dignitary and escorting him back.
One event, after the tribulation
Two stages: the church is raptured before the tribulation
Two stages: the rapture comes partway through the final seven years (midtribulation or prewrath)
Does Revelation chart the course of church history in sequence, from the apostles to the end?

Historicist premillennialists (E. B. Elliott, H. Grattan Guinness, and in many sermons C. H. Spurgeon) read the seals, trumpets and bowls as successive eras, usually applying the day-year principle (Ezekiel 4:6) to the 1,260 days. Futurist historic premillennialists (George Ladd, Craig Blomberg) read most of chapters 4–22 as the climactic events at the end of the age, arguing that the historicist identifications kept changing and could be read only by those with access to European history.
Yes: it is a continuous chart of church history
No: most of it describes a final period still to come
Is Israel a distinct people of God, with future promises (land, throne, national restoration) separate from the church?

Classic and revised dispensationalists (Darby, Scofield, Walvoord, Ryrie) see Israel and the church as two peoples with distinct programs; the church is a 'mystery' (Ephesians 3) not foreseen by the prophets, and God's unconditional covenant promises to Israel must be fulfilled to the nation. Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock, Saucy) still expect a future for national Israel, but see one unfolding kingdom program in which the church already shares the Davidic and New Covenant blessings, so that Israel and the church are distinct but not separate. (Covenant theologians and progressive covenantalists would see the church as the fulfilment of Israel, but few of them hold a pre-tribulation rapture.)
Yes: Israel and the church are two peoples with distinct programs
Israel has a national future, but the church shares already in one kingdom program
Will the gospel substantially Christianize the nations before Christ returns?

Postmillennialists answer yes. They read the Great Commission as a command to disciple nations, not just individuals, and point to kingdom parables of growth (the mustard seed and the leaven), the stone that fills the earth (Daniel 2), Christ reigning until all enemies are subdued (Psalm 110; 1 Corinthians 15:25), and prophecies of the earth filled with the knowledge of the Lord. Amillennialists answer no. They see the wheat and tares growing together until the harvest, expect suffering as the church's normal lot until the end, and note warnings of a final apostasy and of lawlessness increasing (2 Thessalonians 2; 2 Timothy 3). Many still expect real gospel growth, but not a Christianized world.
Yes: the gospel will prevail among the nations before the end
No: good and evil grow together, and the church suffers until Christ returns
Did the Great Tribulation of Matthew 24 take place in AD 66–70?

Partial preterists answer yes. Jesus was answering the disciples' question about the temple's destruction (Matthew 24:1-3), and 'this generation' (24:34) means his contemporaries, as it does elsewhere in Matthew. Luke's parallel (21:20) says 'Jerusalem surrounded by armies', and the 'coming on the clouds' is prophetic judgment language (Isaiah 19:1). Those who answer no argue that the cosmic signs, the worldwide gathering of the elect and the visible coming did not happen in AD 70, or that 'generation' can mean 'race' or the generation that sees the signs. Historicist postmillennialists such as the Puritans spread tribulation and Antichrist imagery across church history instead.
Yes: it was fulfilled in the Jewish War and the fall of Jerusalem
No, or only partly
Does Revelation chart church history in sequence, toward a future era of gospel triumph?

Puritan and later historicist postmillennialists (Thomas Brightman, John Owen, Jonathan Edwards) read Revelation as a chronological map: the fall of the papal Antichrist and the conversion of the Jews would usher in the millennial 'latter-day glory'. Others who expect the gospel to triumph read Revelation symbolically, as a portrait of Christ's victory throughout the age rather than as a timetable. B. B. Warfield, for example, read Revelation 20 as a picture of the intermediate state while holding postmillennial hopes on other grounds.
Yes: it maps church history, and the latter-day glory is still ahead
No: it portrays Christ's victory symbolically, not as a timetable
Was the Great Tribulation of Matthew 24 fulfilled in AD 66–70?

Some amillennialists (Jay Adams and others) read the Olivet Discourse and much of Revelation preteristically, as fulfilled in the first-century judgments on Jerusalem and Rome. Many others read Matthew 24 as a blend: AD 70 is a real fulfilment, but also a pattern of tribulation that characterizes the whole age and intensifies before the end. Still others regard the Great Tribulation as primarily an end-time event.
Yes: it was fulfilled in AD 66–70
Partly: AD 70 begins a pattern of tribulation that runs to the end
No: it mainly lies at the end of the age
How does Revelation's sequence of visions relate to history?

Idealist and eclectic amillennialists (William Hendriksen, G. K. Beale, Dennis Johnson) see 'progressive parallelism': seals, trumpets and bowls each retell the whole age from a different angle, ending at the final judgment. That is why Revelation 20 can return to the first advent. Many Reformation-era Protestants (Luther, and the Reformers who followed Augustine's present millennium) read Revelation historically, as a chart that names the papacy as Antichrist. Other amillennialists (for example Anthony Hoekema and Kim Riddlebarger) emphasize that the 'signs of the times' run throughout the age but culminate in a personal Antichrist and a final tribulation, reading much of the book's climax as still future. A Christ-centred 'spiritual understanding' reads the visions chiefly as an unveiling of Christ's finished work and of present spiritual realities (union with Christ, the renewed mind, the two cities).
Parallel cycles: each retells the whole church age in symbols
A chronological chart of church history
Mainly a picture of the end-time climax, with patterns that run through the age
They unveil Christ and his finished work as present spiritual realities
Full preterism (covenant eschatology)

You read every eschatological promise as fulfilled when the old covenant age ended in AD 70: the Parousia, the resurrection (usually understood corporately or as believers receiving immortal bodies at death) and the judgment. The new creation is the ongoing new covenant order. Advocates include Max King and Don Preston. This view sits outside the historic creeds, which confess a future bodily return and resurrection. Critics, including many partial preterists, also argue from 1 Corinthians 15 and Acts 1:11; proponents respond that the creeds must yield to the New Testament's time texts.
Historic premillennialism (post-tribulational, futurist)

You expect a future Great Tribulation that the church will pass through, followed by one glorious return of Christ, the resurrection of believers and an earthly millennial reign before the final judgment. The view sees one people of God and an inaugurated kingdom (already/not yet). It has roots in the second-century Fathers and modern defenders such as George Ladd, Craig Blomberg and Wayne Grudem.

You read Revelation as a chart of church history, typically using the day-year principle, and expect Christ to return before an earthly millennium. This was a major nineteenth-century Protestant view (E. B. Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae, H. Grattan Guinness, with C. H. Spurgeon sharing its premillennial and historicist outlook), and Seventh-day Adventism inherits a form of it.
Premillennialism with a prewrath or midtribulation rapture

You expect the church to face part of the final seven years, including the Antichrist's persecution, and to be raptured before God's wrath in the Day of the Lord. That is followed by Christ's return to earth and a millennial reign. Prewrath advocates (Marvin Rosenthal, Alan Kurschner) are futurist premillennialists. Some retain dispensational distinctives about Israel and others do not, so this result sits between the historic and dispensational forms.
Dispensational premillennialism (pre-tribulational, futurist)

You distinguish Israel and the church, expect the church to be raptured before a future seven-year tribulation (Daniel's seventieth week), and look for Christ's return to establish a literal thousand-year kingdom centred on restored national Israel. Classic and revised dispensationalists such as John Walvoord, J. Dwight Pentecost, Charles Ryrie and Thomas Ice defend this, citing a consistently literal reading of prophecy.
Progressive dispensational premillennialism

You expect a pre-tribulation rapture, a future tribulation and an earthly millennium with a restored national Israel, but see the Davidic and New Covenant promises as already inaugurated in Christ and shared by the church. Israel and the church are distinct but not separate peoples of God. Representatives include Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy.
Postmillennialism + partial preterism

You read the Olivet Discourse's tribulation and much of Revelation (dated before AD 70, a disputed date) as fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem, and expect the gospel to disciple the nations over the long millennial age before Christ's one bodily return, the general resurrection and the final judgment. Leading modern representatives include Kenneth Gentry, Greg Bahnsen, Gary DeMar, Keith Mathison and Douglas Wilson.
Historicist postmillennialism (Puritan)

You read Revelation as a map of church history, with Antichrist's fall and a future conversion of the Jews ushering in a 'latter-day glory' of worldwide gospel success before Christ returns. This was the dominant hope of many Puritans and of Jonathan Edwards, and it drove the early modern missionary movement (as traced in Iain Murray's The Puritan Hope).
Postmillennialism + idealist or eclectic reading

You expect the gospel to triumph among the nations before Christ returns, but read Revelation symbolically, as a portrait of Christ's victory in the church age rather than a timetable. B. B. Warfield combined postmillennial optimism with a symbolic reading of Revelation 20, and Loraine Boettner's case rested more on the broad sweep of Scripture than on a particular scheme for Revelation.
Amillennialism + partial preterism

You see the millennium as the present reign of Christ and read the Great Tribulation and much of Revelation as fulfilled in the first century, without expecting the nations to be Christianized before the end. Jay Adams's The Time Is at Hand is a classic statement. R. C. Sproul held partial preterism while remaining undecided between amillennialism and postmillennialism.
Amillennialism + idealist or eclectic reading

You read Revelation as parallel cycles that span the whole age between Christ's comings, rooted in a first-century setting and climaxing in a real final judgment. The millennium is Christ's present reign. Representatives include William Hendriksen (More Than Conquerors), G. K. Beale and Dennis Johnson.
Amillennialism + historicism (Reformation pattern)

You see the millennium as the present (or, for some Reformers, an already-past) age, while reading Revelation and Daniel as a chart of church history that identifies the papacy as Antichrist. This combination was common among sixteenth-century Reformers, including Luther, who followed Augustine on the millennium while applying the historicist reading to their own day.
Spiritual understanding (Christ-centred)

You read Revelation as 'the revelation of Jesus Christ': the slain Lamb is the key, the cross is the decisive victory, and the symbols describe present spiritual realities such as union with Christ, the renewed mind, the seal of the Father's name, and the old order of law and self-effort giving way to grace and the new creation. The thousand years are Christ's reign now and the first resurrection is the new birth. You read from victory rather than toward fear, and most who hold this view expect Christ's appearing to consummate what the cross finished. It draws on the spiritual exegesis of Origen, Tyconius and Augustine, and overlaps with idealist, preterist-leaning, amillennial and postmillennial readings. Critics warn that it can allegorise the symbols and underplay the future hope.
Amillennialism with a future climax

You see the millennium as the present age and Satan as bound now, while expecting a final intensification: a personal Antichrist, a last tribulation and apostasy, then one Second Coming, resurrection and judgment. Anthony Hoekema, Kim Riddlebarger and Sam Storms represent this 'signs of the times' amillennialism, though most also use idealist or eclectic readings of Revelation's structure.
Kenneth L. Gentry Jr.
Reformed Presbyterian minister and author

Gentry is the leading contemporary scholarly advocate of postmillennialism joined to partial (orthodox) preterism. His doctoral work, published as Before Jerusalem Fell, argues at length that Revelation was written under Nero before AD 70, and he reads most of Revelation's judgments as fulfilled in the Jewish War. He Shall Have Dominion is his systematic defense of postmillennial optimism grounded in the covenants, the Great Commission and Christ's present reign. He has represented postmillennialism and preterism in several multi-view volumes and debated Thomas Ice in print, while also writing against full preterism, which he regards as outside creedal orthodoxy.
Greg L. Bahnsen
Orthodox Presbyterian; Van Tillian apologist and theonomist

Bahnsen was a philosopher, apologist and Orthodox Presbyterian minister best known for presuppositional apologetics and for theonomy, the view that the moral and judicial laws of the Old Testament remain normative. He was a convinced postmillennialist who taught that the gospel, working through the church and the means of grace, will bring the great majority of the world to faith before Christ returns. His lectures on the subject were published posthumously as Victory in Jesus. With Kenneth Gentry he wrote House Divided, a sustained reply to dispensational critics of Reconstructionist postmillennialism.
Loraine Boettner
Presbyterian (Princeton-trained) lay theologian

Boettner, trained under the Old Princeton theologians, wrote the mid-twentieth-century standard defense of postmillennialism at a time when the view had largely fallen out of favour. The Millennium surveys the three millennial positions and argues that the world will be Christianized through the ordinary preaching of the gospel, leading to a long era of righteousness and peace before Christ returns. He represented postmillennialism in Robert Clouse's The Meaning of the Millennium (1977). He is also known for The Reformed Doctrine of Predestination.
B. B. Warfield
Old Princeton Presbyterian

Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield was the leading Princeton theologian of his generation. His essay The Millennium and the Apocalypse reads Revelation 20:1-10 not as a future earthly era but as a picture of the blessedness of departed saints reigning with Christ in heaven during the present age, an exegesis many classify as amillennial or idealist. Yet his broader eschatology was strongly optimistic: he expected the gospel to win the world before the end, and he argued that the vast majority of humanity would finally be saved. He is therefore claimed by both postmillennialists and amillennialists, and his label is disputed.
